## Study: Air War (`studies/air-war.md`)

### Summary — the state of the area now

The air war in this record is history's air war with two new instruments in it, and its shape is set by one fact: American air power became far better at destroying what it could measure, and the enemy, within a season each time, stopped owning anything that could be measured. The two instruments arrived on the war's first day. The first was eyes: two U-2S Dragon Ladies and four RQ-4B Global Hawks (P003a, P003b), working under the standing condition that gives them GPS and satellite links (E01), so that from January 1964 the enemy's roads, passes, fuel dumps, missile sites and assembly areas were watched in any weather and counted every night. The second was a hand: every B-52 replaced one for one by the re-engined B-52J with the AN/APQ-188 radar (P005a), carrying the GBU-31 and GBU-38 Joint Direct Attack Munitions (P005b, P005c) and the Quickstrike family of influence mines (P005d), and fed from March 1964 by a coordinate cell at Tan Son Nhut under Major Edwin T. Sorrell that turned imagery into aimpoints true to a few metres (EV005-1).

Between them they changed four things, and each change was real. First, the war's interdiction debate became honest five years early: the panhandle watch counted the Trail's trucks from December 1965 (EV003-3), the Sihanoukville count settled in March 1967 an argument history settled only with captured ledgers in 1970 (EV003-4), and from 1969 every Commando Hunt claim travelled to Washington beside a radar count that never let the claim that more trucks had died than existed survive a season (EV000-55, EV000-68). Second, a siege the enemy dug became the enemy's worst battle: Con Thien lifted about three weeks early in 1967, Khe Sanh about two weeks early in 1968 with perhaps 3,500–4,000 PAVN dead to July against about 2,469 acknowledged, and in 1972 the J's cells broke the penetration of An Loc on 12 May and the assault on Kontum short of the wire (EVCP02-3, EV000-41, EV000-76, EV000-77) [X-005]. Third, the air war over the North, when Washington finally allowed it in 1972, chose from folders seven years in the making: the Thanh Hoa bridge fell on the first night of Freedom Train, and Linebacker II cost about six bombers rather than fifteen and did not hit Bach Mai or Kham Thien Street (EV000-75, EV000-82) [X-005]. Fourth, a handful of single events went the other way from history because a radar watched them: Pierce Arrow was never flown after the false alarm of 4 August 1964, and Neak Luong was never bombed in August 1973 (EV000-3, EV000-86).

None of that reached the three things that decided the war, and the record says so as plainly as it records the gains. The enemy's flow south was taxed, never stopped. HARD CROSSING cut every bridge in the panhandle in 1966 and taxed the flow by 10–15 percent for a few weeks; by the autumn Group 559 had built a braided net of fords, causeways and pontoons with no single point of failure, and from then on the panhandle was harder to cut than history's ever was (EV005-2, POS005-4). The study judges tonnage arriving in the South a trace below history's at most in every phase from 1966 to 1972, and the Trail's capacity one to three points above history's from 1966 to the end, which is the measured price of the J's precision against a labour-rich enemy (G-9). The main force under canopy was found no better than history found it, and the air war's precision added nothing against it (POS003-1, POS005-1). And none of the instruments belonged to the Republic. The U-2S, the Global Hawks, the cell, the folders and the bombers all went home in 1973; the Joint General Staff asked to keep a coordinate cell and there was nothing in the VNAF for it to send coordinates to (EV000-86). The ARVN had learned, at Lolo and Sophia, An Loc and Kontum, to hold a besieged position and wait for the bombs, and in 1974 it waited at Thuong Duc for a siege box that no longer existed (EV000-91). At Phuoc Long the province chief's plan asked for "the B-52 support provided for in the plan" by the call signs of 1972 (EV000-92).

So the margin over history is large inside the air war and small outside it. Over the North and on the Trail it is a better-informed, more precise and less costly version of the same campaign against the same rules, with the same result. In the South it is a set of besieged positions held more cheaply while the Americans were there and an army more dependent on them when they left, which the study judges as the Republic's own fire support standing up to three points below history's at the end of 1972 (P5). The one place the air war's balance turns in the Republic's favour is late and indirect: in 1974–75 a larger appropriation kept a third more of the VNAF flying, and its transports and helicopters carried the relief of Phu Loc, the counter-attack at Phuoc An and three weeks of the siege of Pleiku (EV000-91, EV000-95). At the end of 1975 the Republic still has an air force, which history's did not, and it still cannot break a siege with it. The gap register's sentence on air power stands at its true weight in both directions: decisive against the measured siege and the fixed crossing, nothing against a regiment under canopy or an attack on a post at night, and none of it Vietnamese (G-12).

Memoranda 014 and 015, folded at CP04, change one clause of this summary and confirm the rest. The verdict that air power did nothing against an attack on a post at night, and that none of it was Vietnamese, no longer holds as written. From January 1964 a post on a clear night within the net had an AC-130J over it in 15–30 minutes (EV015-1), and from 1969 the VNAF's radar-carrying AC-130Us answered about two-thirds of the posts through cloud and went on answering them after 1973 (EV015-6, EV015-8). The first clause stands and gains a sentence: the gunships could not fly over the PAVN's divisions in 1974–75 (EV000-91, EV000-95). Delta's reconnaissance teams brought the war its first coordinates measured from under the canopy, 134 of them in 1966–67, and Group 559 answered them as it had answered the J, by dispersing what could be measured (EV014-4, POS014-2). The VNAF at the end of 1975 can lift, resupply, strike with unguided bombs and hold a post at night. It still cannot break a siege.

### P1 · Phase I — The advisory war and escalation (Jan 1964 – Jul 1965)

The air war of Phase I was an air war of watching and waiting, and its most consequential sortie was one that was not flown. The two U-2S and four Global Hawks flew from January 1964 (P003a, P003b). On 3 March 1964 Sorrell opened the coordinate cell in a Quonset hut beside Major Harold Kessling's exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut, with eleven officers and twenty-six enlisted analysts, and its first discovery was that every map in the country was wrong: the Army Map Service's 1:50,000 sheets sat on the Indian 1960 datum, several hundred metres off the satellites' truth at Tan Son Nhut and 300 metres or more in the panhandle's mountains (EV005-1, F005-19) [X-005]. His memorandum of 14 May 1964, that no coordinate taken from a map was to be given to a guided weapon, became the cell's law for a decade. On Guam the 3960th Strategic Wing took delivery of its first B-52Js with GBU-31 and GBU-38 kits in storage that spring and trained on ranges in the Marianas [X-005]. By June 1965 the cell held about 1,400 folders, every road and rail bridge between the 20th parallel and the DMZ, the ferries on the Song Ca, Song Giang and Kien Giang, the Mu Gia and Ban Karai passes and the first truck parks in Laos, and no folder had been struck [X-005]. A quarter to a third of the U-2S's hours went to re-imaging known targets rather than searching for new ones (F005-9).

The decisive night was 4 August 1964. At Admiral Sharp's request a Global Hawk had moved to the Gulf of Tonkin the day before, and when USS *Maddox* and USS *Turner Joy* fired for two hours at radar contacts in thunderstorms, Kessling's log showed the destroyers, a cluster of fishing junks 30 nautical miles west, rain cells, and no fast craft within 40 nautical miles (EV000-3) [X-003]. McNamara told the President so in the early afternoon; Johnson held the strike order and cancelled it at about 1900 [X-003]. Pierce Arrow's 64 sorties against the torpedo-boat bases and the Vinh oil storage were not flown, Lieutenant (jg) Richard Sather was not killed over Hon Gai, and Lieutenant (jg) Everett Alvarez was not taken prisoner that day [H] [X-003]. The Southeast Asia Resolution passed anyway on 10 August, on the real attack of 2 August, 414–0 and 85–3 [X-003]. The air war's legal foundation was the same; its first pretext was gone.

The rest of the phase ran on history's dates for history's reasons (EVCP01-2). Barrel Roll began over northern and eastern Laos on 14 December 1964 and Steel Tiger over the panhandle on 3 April 1965, under the ambassador's control of targets and the fiction of Laotian neutrality, against a Trail that was still largely porters and bicycles (EV000-6) [H24]. After Pleiku on 7 February 1965, Flaming Dart struck Dong Hoi, Chanh Hoa and Chap Le; Rolling Thunder opened on 2 March with 104 USAF aircraft at Xom Bang and 19 VNAF A-1s at Quang Khe, the only VNAF strike the record names before 1974, and to 24 December 1965 flew 54,139 sorties and lost 180 aircraft [H9] [H5].

Washington refused every request to use the new bombers over the North (EVCP02-2). On 3 April 1965 Lieutenant Colonel Robinson Risner's 79-aircraft package failed to drop the Ham Rong bridge at Thanh Hoa; MiG-17s of the 921st Fighter Regiment shot down two F-105s the next day [H16]. The folder for Ham Rong had been complete since the previous August, and Sharp forwarded on 6 April a request for four Js to release forty GBU-31(V)3/B penetrators from twelve miles out; it was refused on 13 April, and again in June, because the B-52 was a strategic force whose use over the North would be read in Moscow and Peking as escalation (F005-12) [X-005]. The SA-2 sites were seen coming: change detection on 22 March, the first Fan Song emissions on 18 April, eleven prepared sites mapped by 24 July [X-003]. McNamara declined to strike them, for fear of killing Soviet technicians, as he had historically. When an SA-2 shot down Captain Roscoe Fobair's F-4C on 24 July, the retaliation of 27 July was re-targeted from an empty site to the occupied one on the U-2S's pass of the day before, destroyed two launchers and the Fan Song van, and lost two F-105Ds [X-003].

The first Arc Light, on 18 June 1965, was thirty B-52Js from Andersen with no tankers, so the mid-air collision that killed eight crewmen historically did not happen (F005-11); twenty-eight aircraft struck a suspected base near Ben Cat, two of them with twenty GBU-31s each on four huts the U-2S had imaged, and found them empty for days [X-005]. It was the find-and-fix problem in its purest form, and the precision changed none of it (F005-7). The enemy's one blow at the air war on the ground fell at Bien Hoa on 1 November 1964, where a mortar round holed the U-2S in maintenance and cut the panhandle's daily deep look to twice a week until 20 December (EVCP01-3) [X-003]. At the end of July 1965 the North's air defence was an integrated system of guns, MiGs, radar and missiles, every part of it on a map in Saigon and a weapon able to strike every part of it waiting on Guam (F005-13).

**Memorandum 013 (folded at CP03).** The folders this study describes as unstruck until 1972 were struck in one week. Operation HAMMER FALL, 2–9 March 1965, took the North's power, bulk fuel, the Doumer and Ham Rong bridges, Phuc Yen and most of the 921st Regiment's MiG-17s, the warning and fire-control radars and Haiphong's cranes, for no bombers and seven tactical aircraft lost (EV013-1). The SA-2 sites were struck as they were built, and the first missile kill came on 22 August rather than 24 July (EVCP02-2). About 15–40 fewer aircraft were lost over the North in March–July 1965. The North answered as a society, not as an economy: drums, village diesels, pontoons and a fighter force based in China (EV013-2).

### P2 · Phase II — The main force war (Aug 1965 – Dec 1967)

Phase II is where the air war learned its two lessons, and it learned them in the order that would cost most. The first was learned over the Trail. On 6 December 1965, the day Tiger Hound opened, the Global Hawk orbit moved to a racetrack over the Mekong side of the panhandle west of Tchepone, and STEADY COUNT began: tracks of six or more vehicles passed from the exploitation cell to the 2nd Air Division, from April 1966 the Seventh Air Force, and the airborne command post, which sent A-1Es of the 602nd Air Commando Squadron, B-57Bs, F-100Ds, F-105Ds and from February AC-47 gunships (EV003-3) [X-003]. Of about 1,900 tracks in five months, aircraft reached about one in six within forty minutes, attacked one in ten and destroyed or damaged trucks in one in twenty; the pilots claimed about 560 trucks and the cell counted about 210; nine US aircraft were lost, most to 37mm guns Group 559 moved to the passes from January [X-003]. Southbound movements through Mu Gia rose from about 20 a night in December to about 120 in March, and J-2 estimated 70–90 tons a day reaching the South at the peak, more than the forces there required from the North [X-003]. By February the drivers had learned the orbit's changeover hours and began to trellis the open stretches (F003-4). It was the first count of the Trail anyone had made, and it said that the bombing raised the toll without lowering what arrived (POSTNA-4).

On 12 April 1966 Washington authorised the J with the GBU-31 against fixed crossings in the panhandle and in Route Package 1 below the 18th parallel, and Operation HARD CROSSING began: eight Js of the 4133rd Bombardment Wing (Provisional) put 160 GBU-31s on eleven targets that night, and every one was down by dawn through low cloud (EV005-2) [X-005]. For six weeks the crossings stayed down; the Mu Gia bypass was cut for the fourth time in sixteen days on 28 April, the counts at the entry gates fell through May to about a third of March's, and the tonnage south of Tchepone to about half [X-005]. It was read for a few weeks as the Trail closing. Phan Trong Tue's engineers read it correctly in a season: the bomber could destroy anything it could measure, so Group 559 would own nothing it could measure (F005-16). Fords paved a foot under water, bamboo causeways floated at dusk and sunk at dawn, Soviet pontoon sections hidden under the bank by day: at Ban Laboy the cell counted one ford in April, four in July and nine by October [X-005]. By September the trucks were back to March's level and by October about 15 percent above it. About 210 bridges, ferries and causeways died for about 1,900 kits and no bombers; the tax on the flow was 10–15 percent at its May peak and about 5 percent by October, and what HARD CROSSING built for the enemy was a road net more redundant than history's ever became (POS005-4) [X-005]. The chapter's Mu Gia sentence in STEADY COUNT, written before memorandum 005, still has the trucks moving through the craters twenty hours after the first B-52 strike (Q-3).

The second instrument against the panhandle was the sea. On 26 February 1967 Washington allowed the aerial mining of the North's rivers south of the 20th parallel, and four Js from U-Tapao laid 80 Mk 64 and Mk 65 Quickstrikes in the Song Ca and the Song Giang at Quang Khe in a single pass each (EV005-3) [X-005]. The steel lighters stopped coming south of Thanh Hoa by June; the cargo moved to junks, sampans and Route 1A and Route 15, the radar's count of trucks below Vinh rose 25–30 percent while the tonnage into the panhandle stayed about the same, and the North spent perhaps 15,000–25,000 more porters and road workers on Route Package 1 [X-005]. The study takes the record's own answer to how much less arrived because of it: very little.

Over the North the phase was history's, measured earlier. The U-2S showed in May and June 1966 that the North's fuel was already in drums under the trees, and J-2 told CINCPAC on 14 June that the bulk farms were no longer the system; the POL strikes of 29 June flew regardless, and on 1 August J-2 reported that they had not measurably reduced movement south, three months before the intelligence community said so historically (EVCP02-4, F003-10) [X-003]. Robin Olds's Bolo destroyed seven MiG-21s on 2 January 1967, and the VPAF grew from about 100 interceptors to 180 MiGs by 1968 [H9]. The barrier's sensors were laid where the radar's tracks ended, and Task Force Alpha at Nakhon Phanom took the Global Hawk's tracks by teletype from its first day [X-003]. Rolling Thunder had dropped about 864,000 tons by 31 December 1967 [H9].

The second lesson was learned in the South, at Con Thien. From September 1967 the PAVN besieged the hill by fire from 130mm and 152mm guns north of the Ben Hai, with the 90th and 812th Regiments of the 324B Division entrenched to cover them (EVCP02-3) [H42]. The Global Hawk's second orbit imaged the ground every night from 4 September, and from 11 September cells of three Js with thirty to forty GBU-38s each came every two to three hours; the bombardment of 25 September came at about 600 rounds rather than 1,200, the 812th's trenches that reached 900 metres on 13–14 September were struck by morning, and the siege lifted about three weeks early with perhaps a third fewer Marines killed in September and October [X-005]. Westmoreland took from the hill the lesson that a besieged American base could be made the enemy's worst battle (F005-14). It was true, and it would cost the coastal hamlets of Thua Thien a brigade in January.

The enemy's initiative in the area was the engineering answer of 1966, taken by Group 559 on its own reading in one season and never reversed. The ARVN's place in the air war of the phase is absent: the record shows no VNAF sortie between 1965 and 1974, and the posts of the held belt learned from 1967 to call for fire from district guns rather than men (EV008-4, POS008-4), which is the Republic's only fire support the provisions improved.

**Memoranda 012 and 013 (folded at CP03).** The restrike watch kept the Red River crossings at Hanoi closed to rail on about 290 of 517 days in 1965–66. Its count of targets destroyed fell from about 140 a month to about 35 as the North stopped owning anything worth a GBU-31 (EV013-3, F013-12). The POL strikes of June 1966 were never flown, Bolo killed three MiG-21s rather than seven, and the VPAF fought from Chinese airfields (EVCP02-4). About 40–90 fewer aircraft were lost over the North in 1966–67. In the South, memorandum 012's combined fire-support centres routed American air, Arc Light and the J's boxes to ARVN units through one switchboard. That made American fire more available to the ARVN and no more its own (EC012-3, F012-26). The study's central judgment stands and is strengthened: the flow south was taxed, never stopped, and the bombing of the North did not reach it at all (F013-7).

**Folded at CP04: the canopy, the gunships and Mu Gia.** From 20 October 1965 Delta's teams of five worked the Laotian panhandle under Ambassador Sullivan's limits on depth, target and duration (EV014-4). Of 94 missions in 1966–67, 71 were completed without the team being compromised, and they brought back 84 truck parks, 31 gun positions and 19 storage points measured to a few metres, about a third of them under canopy where neither the U-2S nor the Global Hawk could see anything (F014-11) [M014]. Those points went into STEADY COUNT's track list and the coordinate cell's folders. They did not change what arrived: the teams' cueing taxed the flow by perhaps one to four points more than the radar alone, inside the width the chapters already hold, because a target measured by a man lying 400 metres from it fared no better than one measured from 60,000 feet once the enemy dispersed it (F014-8) [M014]. The cost was nine Americans killed or missing in the panhandle in two years, a whole team of them near the Ban Laboy ford in July 1967.

The Ubon Ghostriders worked the Global Hawk's tracks from December 1965, and for the first time a track had a gun over it within twenty minutes (EV015-3). The video counted 1,100–1,500 trucks killed in the first dry season and 2,000–2,600 in the second, and Group 559 answered with convoys at intervals, parks under the trees and canopy bypasses built a year ahead of history's [M015]. Over the posts the same aircraft answered the held belt's calls in 15–30 minutes on clear nights, and the Front moved its night attacks into the monsoon cloud, where eleven posts fell on the II Corps coast in 1966 under a gunship that could not come down (EV015-4). CP04 also reconciled the opening of HARD CROSSING with STEADY COUNT. On 12 April 1966, the day history's B-52s first struck the Mu Gia pass with unguided bombs, the Js cut the crossings at its foot with GBU-31s, and the orbit watched the first trucks cross again about twenty hours later on a ford the engineers had reopened beside the broken bridges (EV003-3, EV005-2) [X-CP04].

### P3 · Phase III — Tet and its aftermath (Jan 1968 – Dec 1968)

The air war of 1968 won the year's most complete victory on the ground and watched the year decided elsewhere. From mid-December 1967 the panhandle watch tracked the 304th Division's vehicles coming down Route 9 out of Laos, about 20–25 a night rising to about 80 by mid-January; the U-2S's signals payload fixed the 325C Division's headquarters northwest of Hill 881 North on 2 January and the 304th's near Co Roc on 11 January (EV000-41) [X-003]. It was the most complete picture of an enemy concentration the command had ever held, and Westmoreland, after Con Thien, read it on 13 January as the battle the enemy would give him; the radar plots went every evening to the White House and its terrain model (F005-14) [X-005]. The picture showed the border and nothing else. The forces that attacked the cities on 30–31 January moved into them among the Tet crowds, where no radar could tell them from anyone (F003-16) [X-003]. A brigade of the 101st Airborne Division was drawn from the coastal districts of Thua Thien with the 1st Cavalry Division, and was not there when the Front's local forces returned to them [X-005].

Operation Niagara had two halves. The historical half, about 60 B-52s a day on the valleys, the parks and Route 9 in Laos, fell as a carpet half as dense because the J carries about half the D's unguided bombs, about two-thirds of the historical tonnage of unguided bombs (F005-8) [X-005]. The new half was a Global Hawk over the plateau every night imaging the ground within three kilometres of the perimeter each hour, a detachment of the cell moved to Da Nang, and from 26 January cells of three Js every ninety minutes with GBU-38s on positions measured that night; from 15 February they were cleared to bomb 400 metres from the Marines and the 37th Ranger Battalion [X-005]. The 304th Division dug toward the eastern perimeter on 17, 22 and 27 February, and each time its trenches were destroyed at 500–800 metres; on 29 February its regiment formed in the open to assault the Rangers and was broken before the wire [X-005]. The 130mm and 152mm guns rolled out of the caves at Co Roc across the Laotian border were struck within hours of each mission and by mid-March fired only at night. Lang Vei had forty minutes' warning of the twelve PT-76s of the 203rd Armored Regiment on 7 February and fell all the same [X-003]. The air bridge, about 14,356 tons, lost about a third fewer helicopters because the flak around the approaches was struck each night [H46] [X-005]. Major General Tran Quy Hai pulled the 325C back in mid-March and the 304th before the end of the month, about two weeks early; the study takes the record's judgment of about 180 Marines killed against more than 274, and perhaps 3,500–4,000 PAVN dead to July against 2,469 acknowledged [X-005].

The halt ended the northern campaign on 1 November on history's terms. Over three years and eight months Rolling Thunder flew 153,784 USAF and 152,399 Navy and Marine attack sorties and lost 506 USAF, 397 Navy and 19 Marine aircraft over or near the North, and the record carries those figures unaltered (EV000-53) [H9] (Q-1). The Gulf watch, flying over international waters, kept counting: within a week trucks moved by day in columns of forty and fifty, the ferries at Quang Khe ran in daylight, and in December southbound movements on Route 15 toward Mu Gia were about three times October's (EV003-5) [X-003]. The count went to Washington twice a week and changed nothing about the halt, which had been traded for the talks.

It changed the next campaign. Commando Hunt opened on 15 November with Igloo White, the AC-130s of the 16th Special Operations Squadron and, in this war, the Global Hawk as a third sensor and the J as a fourth instrument (EV000-55) [X-003]. The interdiction points at Mu Gia, Ban Karai and Ban Laboy were cut with GBU-31s on measured coordinates rather than cratered by boxes, the Xe Bang Fai and Xe Kong were sown with Quickstrikes set for the steel pontoons, and the tankers freed by the J's range let the F-4s fly about a quarter more sorties a night (F005-10) [X-005]. The points did not close: at Ban Laboy the cell now counted fourteen fords and two underwater causeways [X-005]. The phase's claims ran to 7,322 trucks; the radar counted about 2,600–3,200 destroyed or disabled and a cut of about a sixth in tonnage reaching the South, the J's crossings adding perhaps a fiftieth part of the flow [H53] [X-003] [X-005]. From May 1969 the two figures travelled to Washington together.

The PAVN's own reading of the year, taken by the front command and not provoked by anything new in it, was the clearest enemy initiative of the area: it would not again lay siege to a position the Americans could measure (POS005-1). That was the one way of choosing its battles it had lost, and it chose all the others. The ARVN took a different lesson from Khe Sanh, which it watched rather than fought, and the VNAF appears nowhere in the year's record.

**Memoranda 012 and 013 (folded at CP03).** There was no partial halt, and the summer of 1968 over Hanoi cost about 30–40 aircraft that history's campaign never risked (EV013-6). Rolling Thunder ended on 1 November having lost about 810–880 aircraft rather than 922 (EV000-53). At Hue a single fire centre in the Citadel took every call for naval gunfire, artillery and aircraft, and the battle ended on 27 February rather than 2 March (EV000-44).

### P4 · Phase IV — Vietnamization and drawdown (Jan 1969 – Dec 1971)

Phase IV is the air war turned onto the sanctuaries, and in each sanctuary the precision had a season of targets and then none. On 18 March 1969 forty-eight Js diverted into Cambodia against Base Area 353 in the Fishhook, about 1,600 tons in the boxes rather than 2,400, and twelve aircraft carried 240 GBU-31s onto storage sheds, a vehicle park, a workshop and the clearings where the Global Hawk had seen trucks unload (EV000-58) [X-005]. Menu flew about 3,800 sorties to 26 May 1970; here it dropped about 75,000 tons rather than 108,823, a fifth of the sorties carrying JDAM [H57] [X-005]. About 300 measured structures died in the first six weeks of Breakfast and Lunch; by June COSVN's rear services had moved everything that mattered under the trees and underground, searched the base areas for spies and beacons, found neither, and owned nothing in the open again (F005-16) [X-005]. COSVN itself, a few hundred people under the canopy, was never located. The *New York Times* reported the bombing on 9 May 1969 and the wiretaps followed; in this war they are never exposed, because there is no Watergate (P011a) [X-011]. The study leaves Cambodia's value to the enemy to the study of maritime interdiction, which holds Sihanoukville (see Judgments); the air war's part in it was a season of targets.

The radar's second ledger made Commando Hunt the honest campaign history's never was, and the campaign failed regardless (EV000-68). Phase V, 10 October 1970 to 30 April 1971, claimed 16,266 trucks, which Seventh Air Force itself lowered to 11,000; the radar counted about 4,500–5,500 destroyed or disabled and a net loss to the throughput of about 8–10 percent [H53] [X-003]. The DIA model that historically reached zero trucks fourteen times in 1969 never reached the Secretary of Defense, because the radar showed every night the trucks it said did not exist. By 1970 the cell's folders held about 4,000 crossings, a third in use on any night; the Quickstrike fields on the Xe Kong and the Se San kept the pontoons and barges off the rivers, so the fuel drums floated down on bamboo rafts; and the one target that could not move, the pipeline from Vinh toward the A Shau, had its pumping stations cut about eighty times between October 1970 and the end of 1971 and bypassed within two to four days each time by flexible pipe around the crater [X-005]. The study takes the record's judgment that the J raised the net loss by one or two points at the season's peak [X-005]. The Trail's corridor widened from about 30 to about 90 miles, the PAVN built more than 3,000 km of roads, and the count of southbound trucks rose to about 150–200 a night at the 1971 peak [H53] [X-003]. It is the clearest case in the war of a metric improving without the war improving, and in this war this headquarters wrote that sentence in 1969 from its own counts (A13). The record's comparison of the radar's 8–10 percent with the historical estimate of about 2 percent does not say how much of the difference is effect and how much measurement (Q-2).

Lam Son 719 showed what the air war could and could not do for the ARVN once the advisers stayed behind (EV000-71). J-2's estimate of 4 February 1971, from the U-2S's signals and the panhandle watch, put 35,000–40,000 men within reach of Tchepone, about twice the planners' historical figure, and the operation went ahead on its date [X-003]. Sorrell's detachment at Quang Tri, a dozen Americans who could not cross the border, passed measured positions to the Js; the ARVN on the hills passed nothing, because they had no means to give a coordinate a bomber could use (F005-20) [X-005]. At Lolo and Sophia, where the PAVN 2nd Division's regiments dug in from late February, the trenches were struck each night at 400–700 metres and the bases held until evacuated; at Ranger North, Ranger South and Fire Support Base 31, where the 308th and 320th Divisions came straight at the wire in daylight, the bases fell much as they had historically, and on 25 February six of about twenty tanks the radar tracked forming up were destroyed before they reached the hill, which fell that afternoon (F005-6) [X-005]. In the retreat the Js' GBU-38s destroyed about 110 dug-in gun positions around the landing zones, and the study takes the record's judgment of about a sixth fewer of the historical 108 helicopters lost [H56] [X-005]. Hanoi admitted 2,163 killed; the record does not adjust the ARVN's losses, which were decided by the landing zones and the command.

The lesson I Corps drew was the one that would cost it. The bases it had held were the bases where the bombs came every two hours, and it began to build its plans for the defence of the North around them (F005-20). The Republic's only countervailing fire-support gain of the phase was in the Delta and in the plants: at Long My from February 1970 the subsector advisers handed the call for fire to Vietnamese guns on Vietnamese sets (EV008-7), and by the end of 1971 a third of the 105mm rounds were domestic (EV008-6). The VNAF grew on Vietnamization's historical schedule; nothing in the force reached it.

**Folded at CP04: the night net changes hands.** The Ghostriders went home on Vietnamization's schedule, from Bien Hoa in October 1970 and Nha Trang in December 1971, while the 16th at Da Nang and the 17th at Ubon stayed into 1972 (EV015-6). The VNAF's 81st Gunship Wing flew 700–850 sorties a month at its best, at about 55% of its aircraft operational, and covered about two-thirds of the posts the Ghostriders had covered, through cloud on the coast where they never could [X-015]. Over Cambodia the 817th learned the dossier's warning, losing Spooky 34 to a 37mm battery near Snuol on 14 August 1970, and was sent back to the Delta's posts (EV015-7). On the Trail the Ghostriders on the radar's tracks raised Commando Hunt's net loss at the season's peak to about 10–13 percent, against guns that had been on the Trail a year longer than history's; two were lost over the panhandle in 1970–71, and the Trail grew regardless (EV000-68). In Cambodia Delta's 61 foot missions of 1969 counted 94 cache sites and 11 field hospitals under rubber that the radar could not see; the folders are part of why the incursion found the caches in days, and COSVN had gone to Kratie on 19 March 1970 regardless (EV014-7).

### P5 · Phase V — The Easter Offensive and Linebacker (Jan 1972 – Dec 1972)

1972 was the air war's year in this record, the year the instruments of 1964 were finally allowed to do everything they had been built for, and it confirmed exactly what the earlier phases had shown. The armour of the Nguyen Hue offensive was seen before it crossed: from 12 March the Gulf watch tracked tracked-vehicle columns moving south at night on Route 1A and Route 101 from Vinh Linh, and by 25 March J-2 counted about 90–120 armoured vehicles in assembly areas within 20 kilometres of the DMZ; MACV warned I Corps on 27 March (EV000-74) [X-003]. Lieutenant General Lam expected the blow from the west, and the warning changed the 3rd Division's rotation only in part. When the 304th and 308th Divisions came across on 30 March under cloud that grounded the fighter-bombers, the Bs bombed by radar on the crossings of the Ben Hai and the roads south of Gio Linh and destroyed or disabled about 20–30 armoured vehicles before they reached the firebases [X-003]. The firebases fell all the same, Lieutenant Colonel Pham Van Dinh surrendered Camp Carroll on 2 April, and Quang Tri fell on 1–2 May (EV000-78). The radar had seen the tanks; it had not made the 3rd Division steady.

Over the North the folders of seven years were opened (EV000-75). On the night of 10 April twelve Js put 240 GBU-31s on the Ham Rong bridge, the Thanh Hoa rail yards and the tanks at Vinh, in cloud, and the Dragon's Jaw fell into the Song Ma seven years and seven days after the first request to drop it was refused [X-005]. The Paul Doumer bridge was dropped on 10–11 May by F-4s with laser-guided bombs as historically, because the restricted zone around Hanoi stayed closed to B-52s until December. On the night of Pocket Money the Js laid the secondary fields, about 900 Quickstrikes in the approaches to Hon Gai, Cam Pha, Thanh Hoa, Vinh and Dong Hoi and the waterways south of Haiphong, about 200 of them Quickstrike-ERs released more than forty miles out [X-005]; from June the Gulf watch saw the trucks massing at Dong Dang and Lao Cai to replace the sea. Linebacker flew 41,653 missions and lost 134 aircraft, 104 in combat; the record judges, loosely, that the electronic order of battle and the J's work on fixed targets saved perhaps 15–25 of those losses, and that traffic below Vinh in July stood at about 35 percent of March against about 40 percent historically, because the bridges fell in the first week rather than the first month [H68] [X-003] [X-005].

In the South the siege box did what it had done at Con Thien and Khe Sanh, and did it for the ARVN. At An Loc from 15 April a Global Hawk was given the town every night and Sorrell's detachment at Long Binh measured gun positions, bunkers, tank harbours and trenches; from 16 April cells of Js came every two hours with GBU-38s, the nearest 400 metres from Brigadier General Le Van Hung's lines, and the town's shelling came at perhaps two-thirds of history's weight (EV000-76) [X-005]. The assault of 11 May was on the radar from the evening of the 10th, and through the morning of 12 May the cell measured the buildings the 9th Division had taken in the northern town and put GBU-38s on them 300–400 metres from the ARVN line, one aimpoint to a bomb; the penetration was destroyed by noon [X-005]. At Kontum the three weeks after Tan Canh were the B3 Front's to lose: John Paul Vann had a detachment of the cell flown to the airfield on 28 April, it measured about 600 positions in the arc north and west of the city by 13 May, and about a third of the guns the PAVN brought were destroyed before the assault; the 320th Division's 48th Regiment was broken short of the wire on 14 May and Colonel Ly Tong Ba declared the city secure on 4 June, five days early (EV000-77) [X-005]. Tan Canh itself fell in a day to tanks already inside the wire, and nothing in the J reached a fight of that kind (F005-6).

Linebacker II ended the year (EV000-82). The 729 completed sorties were J sorties, a third of them carrying twenty GBU-31s each on measured aimpoints in the rail yards at Kinh No, Lang Dang and Yen Vien, the power plants and the SAM sites; the rest carried the J's unguided load, about 11,000 tons rather than 15,237 [X-005]. The North fired 266 SA-2s [H69]. The first three nights' routes were SAC's, as historically, and the missile crews learned them; the record judges about six Js lost rather than fifteen B-52s, from the later electronic-warfare suite, the higher release and the destruction of the sites at Kinh No and Phuc Yen on the fourth night rather than the eighth, with about thirteen men killed or missing and twelve captured against 33 and 33 [X-005]. Neither Bach Mai hospital nor Kham Thien Street was hit, and the record judges the civilian dead at about 900–1,200 against Hanoi's count of 1,624 [X-005]. The terms were October's.

The PAVN's 1972 losses stand in the record at about 7,000–10,000 above history's, concentrated in the 5th, 7th and 9th Divisions and the 320th and 2nd, most of the difference made by the siege box [X-MT01]. The VNAF, fourth largest air force in the world after Enhance Plus delivered 234 F-5As and A-37s, 32 C-130s and 277 UH-1Hs [S2], is absent from the record's account of every siege. The ARVN ended the year having learned more completely than history's that it held besieged towns with American bombers measured onto the enemy by American analysts (F007-23), and the agreement about to be signed took both away.

**Folded at CP04: the gunships at An Loc.** EV000-76 now says what memorandum 015's null for this phase implied and the chapter omitted. History's AC-119s and AC-130Es did not exist in this war; the night shift over An Loc was flown by the 17th Special Operations Squadron's Ghostriders from Ubon and the 817th's Spooky IIs from Bien Hoa, working between the bomber cells on the sappers, the digging parties and the mortar crews, 50–200 metres from the defenders (F015-3). From the last days of April the SA-7 drove both above 10,000 feet, where their sensors and radar fire control still worked and the closest work at the wire did not [X-CP04]. They changed no part of the siege's course, which the J's cells decided on 11–12 May.

### P6 · Phase VI — Paris, the endgame, and 1975 (Jan 1973 – Dec 1975)

The air war's last phase in this record is the war of its absence, and the absence was felt more sharply than history's because more had been taken away. Until 15 August 1973 the Js went on bombing Cambodia in support of Lon Nol; on 6 August, where historically a B-52 whose navigator failed to set a beacon offset killed about 137 people in Neak Luong, the J released on its own GPS into its box in the forest east of the river (EV000-86) [X-005]. Case–Church passed in the same words and by the same margins, because the vote was not about the President (F011-9). The Js went home to the alert pads at Andersen and U-Tapao and stayed on alert there each dry season as the visible instrument of the President's promise to Thieu [X-011]. Sorrell's cell, folded into the Defense Attaché Office in March, was disbanded in September, and its folders for every firebase and district town in the South went to Clark and then to the Defense Mapping Agency. The Joint General Staff asked to keep a coordinate cell of its own; there was nothing for it to send coordinates to, because no aircraft the VNAF flew could carry a guided bomb (F005-20) [X-005].

The North's air defences moved south with its corps, and its roads were rebuilt on the historical schedule. Resolution 21 of October 1973 set the rebuilding, and the strategic road east of the Truong Son and the pipeline into the South were built as history built them (EV000-87); the study judges the Trail's capacity still one to three points above history's, because they were laid onto a panhandle net that the J had taught to have no single point of failure. The chapter judges tonnage arriving at the end of 1974 about history's, and at the end of 1975 two to five points above it, because the road had a second dry season's offensive to carry.

The ARVN fought 1974 with plans written for an air force that no longer came (EV000-91). At Thuong Duc the 79th Ranger Battalion dug in and waited, as its officers had seen the 23rd Division wait at Kontum, while the 304th Division's regiment dug to the wire in eleven days without a bomb falling, and the town fell on 7 August [X-005]. The Airborne's counter-attacks on Hill 1062 were planned by officers who had held Lolo and Sophia under the Js, and went forward in the expectation that the crest would be broken from the air first; the VNAF's A-37s and F-5As, flying in monsoon cloud with unguided bombs, could not do it, and the record judges the Airborne's losses on the heights perhaps a tenth higher than history's [X-005]. Historically the VNAF placed 224 aircraft in storage in 1974 and cut its flying hours by about half [S1]. In this war a fiscal 1975 appropriation of about $950 million, stretched by the domestic plants, put a third fewer aircraft on the ground by December (P011a) [X-011]; at Phu Loc from 28 August the 1st Division's counter-attack had VNAF UH-1Hs for lift and resupply on most days instead of some, and the hills were retaken in the third week of November rather than on 10 December [X-011].

Phuoc Long was the air war's epitaph (EV000-92). The province chief's plan for Phuoc Binh, drafted in 1973 by officers who had served at An Loc, was to hold for six to eight weeks while the bombers broke the siege, and it named the bomber cells by Hollingsworth's call signs of 1972 [X-005]. On 13 December 1974 he asked III Corps for the B-52 support provided for in the plan; III Corps forwarded it to the Joint General Staff, which forwarded it to the Defense Attaché Office, which had no means to answer it. On 18 December Thieu would not risk a second division in a province he judged he could not hold without American bombers, in those words and with more conviction than history's, because his officers had seen at An Loc and Kontum what the bombers could do [X-005]. The attack itself was the enemy's own initiative and had an author: Lieutenant General Tran Van Tra argued it in Hanoi in November as a test of the American response, against a Politburo more cautious than history's, and won [X-011]. On 7 January 1975 the President asked Congress for authority to use American air power in the event of a major offensive; the request was dead within the month (EV011-2) [X-011]. Hanoi read it rightly: the President wanted to return, and the Congress would not let him.

In 1975 the VNAF flew the Republic's last fights on fuel the appropriation had bought. The counter-attack from Phuoc An toward Ban Me Thuot on 15–18 March went in lifted by VNAF CH-47s and UH-1Hs and was broken by the PAVN 10th Division as history's was (EV000-95) [X-011]. At Pleiku the C-130As and C-123Ks flew from Nha Trang into Cu Hanh by day, about 25–35 sorties a day, until the 968th's 130mm guns closed the runway on 9 April, and the 6th Air Division's A-37s flew from Pleiku itself until that day [X-011]. The siege lasted three weeks, the town fought it without bombers, and about 11,000 of 25,000 regulars and Rangers reached An Khe and Qui Nhon. The supplementals that kept the VNAF flying, about $150 million in March and $175 million in May, bought fuel and rounds and nothing that could carry a guided weapon (EV000-97) [X-011]. At the end of 1975 the Republic holds III and IV Corps and the bases at Bien Hoa, Tan Son Nhut and the Delta, and so it still has an air force, which history's had not by the end of April (EV011-3). It is an air force that can lift, resupply and strike with unguided bombs, and it cannot break a siege. The Js are on alert at Andersen; the statute keeps them there.

**Folded at CP04: the Republic's own night fire, and what kept it flying.** In the ration of 1974 the Joint General Staff put the gunship wing's Binh Thuy detachment first on the fuel list, because it was the one VNAF unit still fully manned. Military Region 9's rice campaign in Chuong Thien, planned on the reading that the VNAF was grounded, met the gunships every night, and about 46 of 64 attacked canal posts held (EV015-8) [X-015]. At Thuong Duc in August 1974 the first Spooky II over the trenches went down with all thirteen of its crew to the 304th Division's own guns and SA-7s (EV000-91), and at Pleiku in April 1975 the 819th made the 320A's assaults about a fifth dearer and lost two aircraft in a night to radar-laid guns (EV000-95). The record traces the wing's fuel in 1974 and not its spares. CP04 judged that the spares came from the appropriation alone and that the wing flew 1974–75 partly by cannibalising grounded aircraft [X-CP04]; the record holds no event on it, and the gap register now carries it.

### Judgments

**Values carried at CP04.** The seven value lines of memoranda 014 and 015 are carried into `[values]` in their units, re-judged against the record as it now stands and unchanged by that re-judgment. Memorandum 014's line for *SANCT.cambodia* in P4 (−2 to 0 battalions) is carried to the study of maritime interdiction instead, which holds that variable's one copy. Phase IV's *ARVN.effectiveness.fire_coordination* is now judged in the chapter (CP04: 0 to 10 minutes faster in the Delta's districts), which answers Q-5 for that phase only. The 45 values withdrawn at CP03 are still withdrawn, and the re-run stays advised.

**Values withdrawn at CP03 (R03).** The study's 45 values were written on the −10..+10 scale, which R03 retired on 25 November 2026. No mapping from that scale to the variables' natural units exists, and checkpoint CP03 did not invent one: it withdrew the values from `[values]` (they are kept in `reviews/CP03/before-studies/`, and the judgments below still describe them in words) and advised a fresh STUDY of this area in units. Until it runs, the study's account of the area stands and its values are unjudged.

**Chapter end vectors judged by this study (amend file, ST01).** *TRAIL.tonnage_arriving* was converted at 0..0 in Phases I–V and is judged here from the record's counts: P1 −1..+1 (the sea route closed and Sihanoukville opened early, EV003-1, EV003-2; the route changed, not the tonnage); P2 −1..0 (HARD CROSSING's tax of 10–15% in May 1966 and about 5% by October, the estuary field's shift to the roads, EV005-2, EV005-3); P3 −1..0 (Commando Hunt's first-phase cut of about a sixth by the radar, the J adding about a fiftieth, EV000-55); P4 −1..0 (the J's one or two points of net loss, EV000-68); P5 −1..0 (traffic below Vinh in July at 35% rather than 40% of March, EV000-75). All are low confidence; none moves a band, which is the record's own verdict that interdiction taxed and never stopped the flow (POSTNA-4, POS005-4). The P6 end vector and snapshot were judged by memorandum 011 and are not re-judged. *ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support* was unjudged in Phases I–V and is judged here: P1 0..+1 (shell bodies from March 1965; the cell serves only American bombers), P2 −1..+1 (district guns answer the posts' calls, EV008-4, against the doctrine of American fire), P3 −1..+1, P4 −2..+1 (Long My's handover, EV008-7, against I Corps' lesson of Lolo and Sophia, EV000-71), P5 −3..0 (An Loc and Kontum held on American coordinates; POS005-2, F007-23). Judging the facet requires the parent's binding facet (DIRR01-3); this study names *fire_support* as the binding facet of *ARVN.self_sufficiency* in Phases I–V, the facet memorandum 011 already named in Phase VI, on the record's consistent finding that the instruments of the conventional war were never the Republic's (POSCP01-2, POSMT01-1). The parent's ranges are left as converted, because judging maintenance, logistics and replacement lies outside this area.

**Left unjudged in the chapters.** *ARVN.effectiveness.fire_coordination* is left unjudged in every phase. The record holds evidence on it, chiefly that the ARVN battalions of Lam Son 719 had no means to give a coordinate (EV000-71) and that the officers of 1972 used American air with an educated staff's precision (F007-23), but a judged facet obliges the study to name the binding facet of *ARVN.effectiveness* in each phase, a judgment across all seven of its facets (anti-armour at Quang Tri, mobile defence in 1975, urban combat at Hue) that a study of the air war cannot make honestly; it is sent to the next checkpoint (Q-5).

**Study-held values.** *AIR.north_effect*: a trace in P1–P3 (folders unstruck; the estuary field's cost in labour), nothing in P4 and P6, +1..+3 medium in P5 (the first-week bridges of Freedom Train). *AIR.north_defences*: a trace in P1 (Spring High re-targeted) and P5 (Kinh No and Phuc Yen on the fourth night), otherwise nil. *AIR.losses*: −1..0 in P1–P4 (Pierce Arrow not flown, Spring High, the Khe Sanh air bridge, Lam Son's helicopters), −2..−1 medium in P5 (Linebacker II's six bombers against fifteen and 15–25 fewer of Linebacker's 134), nil in P6. *STRIKE.responsiveness*: rising from a trace in P1 to +3..+5 medium in P5 as the siege box matured, falling to 0..+1 in P6 when every American instrument was gone. *TRAIL.capacity*: nil in P1, +1..+3 from P2 to the end, the redundant net of POS005-4. *SANCT.laos*: nil in every phase except a trace in P3, when the guns at Co Roc were struck across the border; the sanctuary's value lay in the ground bar, which nothing in the force changed. *VNAF.capability*: 0..+1 low in P1–P5, the only reach being the enlisted and NCO courses shared with the RVNAF (P009b, P010b), which the record never shows at work in the air arm; in P6 +3..+6 low with *close_support* binding, because at the end of 1975 the Republic still has an air force where history's had none, and still cannot break a siege with it; *close_support* 0..+1, *lift* +2..+4 and *maintenance* +2..+4 on the evidence of Phu Loc, Phuoc An and Pleiku and the P011a appropriation, all low. *VNAF.capability.survivability* is left unjudged in every phase: the record holds no evidence on the VNAF against the SA-7 or the 1975 guns beyond the closing of Cu Hanh.

**Tagged and left unjudged.** *SANCT.cambodia* is tagged because Menu and the Sihanoukville count touch it, and left unjudged here: its value to the enemy turns on the Sihanoukville route, which the study of maritime interdiction in this run covers, and one copy of the value should sit there. *POP.civilian_harm* is tagged because the air war's part in it is real in every phase (Arc Light's carpet half as dense, Menu's 75,000 tons rather than 108,823, Linebacker II's 900–1,200 dead against 1,624, Neak Luong spared), and left unjudged because the variable is civilian harm from all sides' operations, and its decisive differences in this record lie outside the air war: My Lai removed (P011c), the Highlands column of 1975 losing about 9,000 civilians against history's 155,000 (EV000-95). A study of the population should hold it (Q-6).

### Questions for the record

- **Q-1** · RESOLVED · EV000-53 now states the northern campaign's losses in this war, about 810–880 rather than 922 (memorandum 013, POS013-3). Asked: EV000-53 (history/chapters/P3.md, origin HIST) carries Rolling Thunder's historical sorties and its 922 aircraft lost unaltered, while P003a and P005a push AIR.losses −1 (memos 003 and 005 manifests) and EVCP02-2 alters the losses of Spring High; no chapter states Rolling Thunder's losses in this war, and the checkpoint should either alter EV000-53 or state that the pushes did not reach the northern campaign before 1972.
- **Q-2** · STANDS · left to the re-run of this study in units, which can state both ledgers in tons. Asked: EV000-68 (history/chapters/P4.md) sets the radar's Commando Hunt V net loss of about 8–10% against "the phases' own historical estimate falling to about 2 percent" and attributes only one or two points to the J; the chapter does not say whether the remaining difference is a better effect (radar-cued gunships) or a better measurement of the same effect, which decides whether TRAIL.tonnage_arriving in P4 should sit nearer −2 than this study's −1..0.
- **Q-3** · RESOLVED · CP04 staged Phase II and restated EV003-3's sentence on 12 April 1966: the Js of HARD CROSSING cut the crossings at Mu Gia that night, and the trucks the orbit watched twenty hours later crossed on a reopened ford, which the next night's Js cut (EV005-2). Asked: EV003-3 (history/chapters/P2.md, written by memorandum 003) still says that on 12 April 1966 "B-52s struck the Mu Gia pass for the first time [H]; the orbit watched the first trucks move through the craters about twenty hours later", which is history's unguided strike; EV005-2 (memorandum 005) has the Js cut every crossing that night and keep them down for six weeks. The STEADY COUNT sentence was never brought into line and should be reconciled at the next consolidation.
- **Q-4** · STANDS · carried to the gap register (CP03 Part 2 §10). Asked: The record holds no account of the air war in northern Laos after December 1964 (Barrel Roll, the Plain of Jars, the Lima Sites), of the air war in the South by tactical aircraft (close air support sorties and their fall with the withdrawal), or of the VNAF between Rolling Thunder's first day and 1974; no variable captures the weight of American air power in the South, and STRIKE.responsiveness measures speed, not weight. Whether to add such a variable is a version change.
- **Q-5** · STANDS · Phase IV judged at CP04 (0 to 10 minutes faster in the Delta's districts, low); the other phases are left to the re-run · the facet now has a unit (minutes from an ARVN call for fire to rounds on target, R03); CP03 did not reach the evidence of 1971–72, and the re-run judges it. Asked: ARVN.effectiveness.fire_coordination is unjudged in every chapter though the record holds evidence on it (EV000-71, EV000-76, EV000-77, EV000-91, F007-23); judging it needs the binding facet of ARVN.effectiveness in each phase, which the next checkpoint should name.
- **Q-6** · STANDS · POP.civilian_harm now has a unit (civilian dead and wounded a year, R03) and still no holder; carried to the gap register. Asked: POP.civilian_harm has no holder: it is pushed by twelve provisions and judged nowhere, and its decisive differences (P011c; the Highlands column of EV000-95) lie outside any study so far; a checkpoint or a study of the population should judge it.

### Sources

[S1] "South Viet Nam Air Force - 1975 - Maintenance and Supply" — GlobalSecurity.org, https://www.globalsecurity.org/military/world/vietnam/rvn-vnaf-1975-1.htm — 224 aircraft placed in storage and flying hours cut by about 51% in 1974; about 1,484 aircraft at the end of December 1974.
[S2] "Operations Enhance and Enhance Plus" — Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operations_Enhance_and_Enhance_Plus — 234 F-5A and A-37, 32 C-130 and 277 UH-1H delivered from October 1972; the VNAF fourth largest air force in the world at the end of 1972.

### Since this study

#### R05 — Revision · 2026-11-25
<!-- since R05 -->
R05 merged several of the events this study cites, without changing any of them. STEADY COUNT (EV003-3), NIGHT LEDGER (EV015-3) and Delta's road watch (EV014-4) are now one event, EVR05-5, which keeps CP04's finding that trucks crossed a reopened ford at the foot of Mu Gia about twenty hours after HARD CROSSING's first night. The estuary field (EV005-3) is now part of EV005-2, and the coordinate cell (EV005-1) is part of HAMMER FALL (EV013-1). The absent Christmas pause (EV013-4) and the buffer's test (EV013-5) are part of EVCP02-4, and Moscow's and Beijing's answer of 1965 (EV013-2) is part of EVCP02-2. The old IDs remain in the chapters as stubs pointing to their new events. No study-held value changes. The study's third question, whether EV003-3 and EV005-2 can stand side by side, now concerns one event and its sequel (EVR05-5, EV005-2), which tell the ford and the braided net in order.

## Variable ledgers

### AIR.losses
- P003a (memo 003) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — An electronic order of battle of the North's radars, and later of its SA-2 sites, built before the strike forces need it; routes planned around what is known rather than learned by losses
- P005a (memo 005) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Modern defensive suite and release outside the light AAA envelope; SA-2 still lethal
- P013b (memo 013) pushes -3..+0 [v1.0.6 scale] (low) — The SAM sites can be struck while being built and the MiG airfields at Phuc Yen and Kep from 1965, two years before history; route packages flown on the theater's timing rather than Washington's
- P015a (memo 015) pushes -8 to +4 [US aircraft lost over the North and Laos in the phase] by the end of P4 (low) — between eight fewer and four more aircraft lost over Laos in 1969–71: the J flies higher and shoots from further out than the AC-130A, but there are more of them on the Trail and each loss is a nine-man crew

### AIR.north_defences
- P003a (memo 003) depends — The U-2 is safe from guns and MiG-17s at 70,000 ft; it is not safe from the SA-2 once the SA-2 arrives
- P003b (memo 003) depends — At 60,000 ft the RQ-4 is inside the SA-2 envelope; once the North has SA-2s it can look into the North only from outside their range
- P005a (memo 005) depends — SA-2 and MiG-21 density sets loss rates over the North
- P005b (memo 005) depends — The 15-mile glide falls inside the SA-2's reach; standoff protects against guns, not missiles
- P013a (memo 013) pushes -3..-1 [v1.0.6 scale] (low) — In March 1965 the North has no SA-2 site operational and about 50–60 MiGs at Phuc Yen; the opening blow catches the radar net and the fighter force on the ground, but Moscow then ships faster
- P013b (memo 013) pushes -2..+0 [v1.0.6 scale] (low) — No sanctuary for the SAM support, the MiG bases or the Hanoi gun belt; offset by Soviet resupply that grows with the threat
- P014a (memo 014) depends — any raid into the North flies through the North's air defences
- P015a (memo 015) depends — the gunship's survival on the Trail ends when 37mm, 57mm, radar-laid guns, the SA-7 and the SA-2 move south, as they did in 1971–72

### AIR.north_effect
- P003a (memo 003) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Target folders, radar and EO imagery of rail, bridges and ports in the North, and same-day damage assessment, so fewer sorties are wasted on targets already down or never there
- P003b (memo 003) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Under the standing condition (E01) an orbit over the Gulf of Tonkin, outside the SA-2 belt, watches the coastal road and rail net from Vinh to Thanh Hoa and the lighter traffic out of Haiphong in any weather; armed reconnaissance is sent to what is moving rather than to where traffic used to be
- P005a (memo 005) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Twenty independently aimed 2,000 lb weapons a sortie in any weather against fixed targets, where Washington allows
- P005b (memo 005) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Bridges, ferries, depots and power plants struck in monsoon cloud with few sorties
- P005d (memo 005) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Inland waterways and coastal shipping south of the 20th parallel mined persistently
- P013a (memo 013) pushes +3..+5 [v1.0.6 scale] (low) — Power, fuel bulk storage, the rail bridges and the airfields fall in the first days, before the North has dispersed anything; the effect on capacity is large and on will uncertain
- P013b (memo 013) pushes +2..+4 [v1.0.6 scale] (low) — Restrike at the repair rate and choice of targets by the theater keep the bridges, power and rail down; the North still moves by night, by sea and by porter

### ARVN.effectiveness
- P001b (memo 001) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Ghost soldiers removed from the rolls: battalions known to be their real strength, rice and pay reaching the men present
- P002b (memo 002) depends — Competent officers drawn to province and district posts leave battalions and regiments; the selection competes with the line for the same few hundred able officers
- P004a (memo 004) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — ARVN infantry matches and outshoots the AK-47 from 1964 instead of mid-1968; faster hits in the first seconds of a contact at 10–50 m, more volume per man, a lighter weapon for smaller soldiers
- P004b (memo 004) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Small but real: a trained marksman in each squad in the open delta and plains country where ARVN does most of its fighting
- P004c (memo 004) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Squad firepower matching the RPD-armed PAVN infantry from 1964
- P006c (memo 006) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Battalion and subsector advice by men selected and trained for it
- P007b (memo 007) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Company and battalion leadership able to plan, coordinate fires and run training
- P007c (memo 007) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Battalions commanded by officers selected for it, kept in command, and removed when they fail
- P008b (memo 008) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Communications down to squad and outpost, and repair turnaround measured in days
- P009b (memo 009) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Every regular recruit trained to a common, demanding standard, and none sent to a unit untrained; marksmanship with P004a and P004c
- P010b (memo 010) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Every regular squad and platoon led by an NCO schooled for his job, in an army whose NCO corps was its thinnest layer; with P009b the trained private now has a trained corporal
- P012a (memo 012) pushes +2..+5 [v1.0.6 scale] (medium) on ARVN.effectiveness.fire_coordination — one fire-support coordination system across the four nations' sectors; ARVN units can draw US and allied fires through a combined centre rather than through an adviser's radio
- P012a (memo 012) pushes +1..+3 [v1.0.6 scale] (low) on ARVN.effectiveness.combined_arms — combined operations planned by one staff put ARVN infantry beside US and ROK armour and artillery on one plan, with ARVN staff officers in the planning
- P015b (memo 015) pushes -15 to -3 [minutes from an ARVN call for fire to rounds on target] by the end of P5 (low) on ARVN.effectiveness.fire_coordination — 3–15 minutes faster from an ARVN call for fire to rounds on target at night by 1972: the gunship crew and the ground unit share a language, a net and a chain of command

### ARVN.self_sufficiency
- P004a (memo 004) depends — M855A1, optics, batteries and URG-I parts all come from the United States; the RVNAF cannot make or repair them at depth, so the rearmament deepens the supply dependence that 1973–75 punished
- P005c (memo 005) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — Defence of besieged positions is built around an American bomber and American coordinates the RVNAF can never own
- P006c (memo 006) pushes -1 [old band ≈ -4..-2] — An adviser qualified and trusted to call American air and artillery becomes the advised unit's means of fire; better advising of fire deepens the dependence the withdrawal punishes, unless the adviser is directed to train Vietnamese observers to replace him
- P007b (memo 007) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Staff, logistics and fire-support officers educated to run their own systems
- P008a (memo 008) pushes +2 [old band ≈ +5..+7] — Spares, rebuild, cartridge cases and shell bodies made and turned around in country; filling, fuel and major systems still imported
- P008b (memo 008) pushes +2 [old band ≈ +5..+7] — Radios, batteries, wire and signal repair made and done in country; the 1974–75 battery and parts famine eased
- P010b (memo 010) pushes +1 [old band ≈ +2..+4] — Senior and master courses teach maintenance, supply, training management and readiness reporting at company and battalion; the sergeants who keep trucks and radios running
- P010b (memo 010) depends — The schooled squad fights best with American fire and helicopters behind it; in 1974–75 it has been taught a way of war its army cannot supply (F010-24)
- P011a (memo 011) pushes +0..+2 [v1.0.6 scale] (low) on ARVN.self_sufficiency.logistics — Not self-sufficiency but its precondition in 1974: fuel for trucks and rounds for depots that the ration emptied; the dependence on Congress is unchanged
- P011a (memo 011) depends — Aid money matters only as far as the RVNAF can turn it into fire, fuel and spares; the 1974 ration is where the provision bites
- P012a (memo 012) pushes -4..+0 [v1.0.6 scale] (medium) on ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support — an ARVN that plans and fights inside a combined staff learns to depend on it; the staff and its fires leave with the Americans
- P015b (memo 015) pushes +2 to +6 [% of the RVNAF's fire support delivered by its own guns and aircraft] by the end of P4 (low) on ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support — 2–6 points more of the RVNAF's fire support delivered by its own aircraft by 1971: about 400–800 VNAF gunship sorties a month, each worth several hours of night fire, in place of US gunship and tactical air at night
- P015b (memo 015) pushes +3 to +8 [% of the RVNAF's fire support delivered by its own guns and aircraft] by the end of P6 (low) on ARVN.self_sufficiency.fire_support — 3–8 points more of the RVNAF's fire support its own by the end of 1974, if the U is flown and maintained after the Americans leave; bounded by the SA-7 and radar AAA that historically drove VNAF aircraft above useful altitudes
- P015b (memo 015) depends on ARVN.self_sufficiency.maintenance — after 1973 the U flies only as long as the RVNAF's own depots and the aid appropriation keep it in spares

- P003b (memo 003) depends — From South Vietnamese airspace the radar looks 150–200 km into Cambodia and sees the road traffic from Sihanoukville to the border base areas; what it sees there cannot be attacked under the present constraints, but the argument over how the sanctuary is supplied is settled by evidence (F003-3, F003-17)
- P005d (memo 005) depends — Sihanoukville and the Mekong into Cambodia are neutral waters
- P013b (memo 013) pushes +0..+1 [v1.0.6 scale] (low) — With the North's rail and road south battered without pause, Hanoi's freight for B-2 leans harder on the Chinese-flag ships to Sihanoukville that the record already opened in June 1965; the southern route gains as the northern one costs more
- P014a (memo 014) pushes -2 to 0 [enemy main-force battalions based in Cambodia] by the end of P4 (low) — 0–2 fewer main-force battalions based in Cambodia by 1971, revised down against the maritime study and POS003-2, which hold that the sanctuary's value lay in the ground bar that nothing in the force changes, from reconnaissance from 1967 and target-finding for the bombing of 1969 and the incursion of May 1970; Delta cannot enter Cambodia on the ground except as history's forces did
